summary: Defines the string form used in LDAP for distinguished names, the keys that identify entries in an X.500 directory. It reads cleanly for common names but can still represent any distinguished name. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A directory is a list of named entries, and each entry needs a name that points at it and nothing else. This RFC defines the text form of that name, which is what you see in strings like UID=jsmith,DC=example,DC=net, and it explains how to read such a string back into the structure the directory stores.

subtitle: How LDAP writes the name of a directory entry, such as UID=jsmith,DC=example,DC=net, as plain text.

tldr.problem: A directory needs one unambiguous name for each of its entries, but the X.500 way of writing that name is a binary structure that is awkward to encode and decode.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a string form in which the parts of the name are written in order, separated by commas, with each part written as an attribute type, an equals sign and a value, and with special characters escaped.
tldr.outcome: The string form is easy to encode and decode and still readable by people, and the RFC replaced RFC 2253 with it.

facts.label: Separators
facts.value: Comma between parts, plus sign between values in one part

facts.label: Hexadecimal value form
facts.value: A number sign followed by hex pairs

facts.label: Short names all must recognise
facts.value: CN, L, ST, O, OU, C, STREET, DC, UID

today: RFC 4514 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It replaced RFC 2253 and forms part of the LDAP technical specification in RFC 4510, which replaced RFC 3377.

sections.title: What a Distinguished Name Is
sections.content:
In X.500 directory systems, including the ones reached with LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol), a distinguished name (DN) is the primary key of an entry: it names one entry and nothing else. The structure of a DN is defined in ASN.1, and the X.500 Directory Access Protocol encodes that structure with the Basic Encoding Rules. LDAP, being a lighter protocol, uses the string form this RFC defines.

The RFC sets two goals. Ease of encoding and decoding comes first, and human readability second. It does not expect a product with a human interface to show these strings as they are, since the attribute type names are likely to be translated into the user's own language.

The RFC is careful about what it does not define. It does not define a canonical string form for a DN, so two strings that look different may still name the same entry. Deciding whether two names are equal is left to the distinguishedNameMatch matching rule in RFC 4517. This document is an integral part of the LDAP technical specification in RFC 4510, and it obsoletes RFC 2253.
sections.plainLanguage: Every entry in a directory has a full name that identifies it, like a postal address for a person rather than a short nickname. The RFC defines how that name is written in the text that LDAP carries, so that software on both ends can read and write it the same way.

sections.title: From a Stored Name to a String
sections.content:
The stored form of a DN is a sequence of relative distinguished names, and each of those holds one or more attribute type and value pairs. The recommended conversion writes the parts starting with the last element of the sequence and moving backwards, so that the most specific part of the name comes first. Adjoining parts are separated by a comma, and the pairs inside one part are separated by a plus sign.

Each pair is written as the attribute type, an equals sign, and the value. The type is written with its short name when it has one and that short name is registered, for example DC. Otherwise the type is written in the dotted-decimal form of its object identifier, such as 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.0. Implementations are not expected to learn new short names on their own, but they should offer a way to update their list.

The value is written as text when the attribute type has a syntax with an LDAP-specific string form. If the type was written as a dotted-decimal object identifier, or the syntax has no LDAP-specific string form, or that form is not restricted to UTF-8 text, the value is written as a number sign followed by the hexadecimal octets of the BER encoding of the value. The hexadecimal form may also be used in other cases, such as when a reversible representation is wanted.

A text value has to be escaped when it starts with a space or a number sign, ends with a space, contains one of the characters double quote, plus, comma, semicolon, less-than, greater-than or backslash, or contains a null character. Each octet of such a character can be replaced by a backslash and two hexadecimal digits. A smaller set, the space, double quote, number sign, plus, comma, semicolon, less-than, equals, greater-than and backslash, can instead be escaped with a single backslash in front of the character.
sections.plainLanguage: To turn a name into text, the parts are written from the most specific to the least specific, separated by commas, and each part is written as an attribute name, an equals sign, and the value. Characters that would otherwise be confused with the separators are escaped with a backslash.

sections.title: The Grammar of the String Form
sections.content:
Section 3 gives the grammar of the string form in Augmented BNF, and that grammar decides what counts as a valid string. Any algorithm that turns a DN into a string must produce a string that follows it. A distinguished name is a list of relative distinguished names separated by commas. A relative distinguished name is a list of attribute type and value pairs separated by plus signs. Each pair is a type, an equals sign, and a value. The type is either a short name or a dotted-decimal object identifier, and the value is either a string or a hexadecimal string.

Reading the string back works on the escaped pairs from left to right and only once each: a doubled backslash stands for one backslash, a backslash before one of the special characters stands for that character, and a backslash before two hexadecimal digits stands for the single octet those digits describe. A value in hexadecimal form is read the same way, one pair of digits at a time.

Implementations must recognise the attribute type short names in the RFC's table and may recognise others. The table lists CN for commonName, L for localityName, ST for stateOrProvinceName, O for organizationName, OU for organizationalUnitName, C for countryName, STREET for streetAddress, DC for domainComponent and UID for userId. Because implementations may accept other forms, they should only produce strings that follow the algorithm in Section 2.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC writes the rules for these names as a grammar, so that a program can check whether a piece of text is a valid name and can take it apart again. It also lists the short names that every implementation has to understand, such as CN for a common name and DC for a domain component.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The RFC's examples show the notation in use. A name made of three relative distinguished names is UID=jsmith,DC=example,DC=net. When the first relative distinguished name holds two values, they are joined with a plus sign: OU=Sales+CN=J. Smith,DC=example,DC=net.

Special characters inside a common name are escaped with a backslash, as in CN=James \"Jim\" Smith\, III,DC=example,DC=net. A carriage return inside a value is written in the hexadecimal form, as in CN=Before\0dAfter,DC=example,DC=net.

When the attribute type is not one the reader recognises, the hexadecimal form carries the whole value: 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.0=#04024869, where the hexadecimal part is the BER encoding of a string of two octets.

The last example uses characters that have no printable ASCII form. The RFC lists the characters of a common name, their code points and their UTF-8 octets, and shows that the name can be written for a person to read as CN=Lu\C4\8Di\C4\87, where each escape stands for one octet of the UTF-8 encoding of one character.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show how names look in practice, including names with a comma inside a value, a line break inside a value, and letters from outside the ASCII character set. In each case the rule is the same: the separator characters are escaped so they cannot be mistaken for separators.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security section is about what a name itself reveals. Distinguished names usually describe the entry they name, and that description often contains the common name of the object, such as a person's full name, an email or TCP/IP address, a physical location such as country, locality, city or street address, and organisational attributes such as a department name or affiliation.

Some of that information can be sensitive, and privacy laws in many countries forbid disclosing certain kinds of it, email addresses being the example the RFC gives. Server implementers are therefore encouraged to support Directory Information Tree structural rules and name forms, which give administrators a way to choose the attributes that go into the name of an entry, and to use access controls and the authentication and data security services of LDAP to restrict what is exposed.

The second part is about names used in security applications. Turning an attribute value into an LDAP string is not always reversible: a value of 'Sam' held as a TeletexString and the same value held as a PrintableString both become CN=Sam. An application that has to rebuild the exact encoded form, such as one verifying an X.509 certificate, should not rely on the string form of an attribute's syntax and should use the hexadecimal form prefixed by a number sign instead.
sections.plainLanguage: A directory name often spells out who a person is, where they work and how to reach them, so names can carry personal information that privacy rules protect. The RFC also warns that the text form of a name does not always keep the exact bytes it came from, so software that must reproduce those bytes exactly should use the hexadecimal form.

sections.title: Showing Names to People
sections.content:
The last appendix is informational rather than part of the specification, and it gives guidance for software that shows names to people. Not every interface can display every character, so human interfaces are advised to escape everything that is not printable, using the hexadecimal pairs of the octets.

A name is often shown inside angle brackets so that it stands out from the text around it. The RFC notes that the brackets are not part of the name, and that an angle bracket inside a name has to be escaped, which is how a careful reader can tell where the name ends.

Long names are often wrapped over several lines for readability, but whitespace added for wrapping is not part of the name and has to be removed before the name is used. The RFC advises against inserting whitespace, because a reader cannot easily tell which whitespace belongs to the name and which was added. It offers the LDAP Data Interchange Format, LDIF, as the alternative: a long name is written over two lines and the continuation is indented.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC closes with advice for programs that show these names on screen: escape what cannot be printed, wrap long names carefully, and remember that any extra spaces used for layout are not part of the name and must be removed before the name is sent to a server.

data.title: distinguishedName
data.code:
distinguishedName = [ relativeDistinguishedName
    *( COMMA relativeDistinguishedName ) ]
relativeDistinguishedName = attributeTypeAndValue
    *( PLUS attributeTypeAndValue )
attributeTypeAndValue = attributeType EQUALS attributeValue
attributeType = descr / numericoid
attributeValue = string / hexstring
